newsitem.title: KENYA: U.S. secretary of state on belated Africa trip.
newsitem.headline: U.S. secretary of state on belated Africa trip.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher arrives on his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa on Monday, facing widespread scepticism about his motives and what he may achieve.

African analysts said Washington had little interest in most non-Arab parts of the continent and suspected the prime motive for the tour was to boost President U.S. Bill Clinton's share of the Afro-American vote in the November 5 presidential election.
"Where was Christopher all these years? The answer to 'why now?' is votes at home," a former senior Kenyan official told Reuters.
"There will be many polite words, a few photo opportunities and nothing much will change," he added. "The region is boiling. But I can't see much achieved from one visit in four years."
Even planning for the trip to the world's poorest continent was largely dependent on Middle Eastern twists and turns which have dominated Christopher's three-and-a-half years in office.
"The American ambassador said last week that he wouldn't be surprised if he didn't turn up at all because of Middle East problems," said a diplomat in Tanzania's capital Dar es Salaam.
The 70-year-old secretary of state's itinerary surprised some experts -- Mali, Ethiopia, Tanzania, South Africa and Angola. They saw him shunning hot-spots.
In South Africa, Vernon Seymour of the Centre for Southern African Policy Studies at University of the Western Cape said the timing must be linked with the election.
"Afro-American support has been on the wane for the Clinton administration...Christopher's had four years to demonstrate his support for human rights and democracy in Africa," he said.

"One would like to believe that the visit is related to the promotion of democracy in Africa but unfortunately U.S. policy has been so inconsistent, one is sceptical when one sees these African safaris."
However, Richard Cornwell of the Pretoria-based Africa Institute said the commitment of Afro-Americans to Africa was not deep and felt the decision to visit Africa was curious.
Christopher arrives on Monday in Mali and meets President Alpha Oumar Konare to encourage progress towards democracy.

His stop in West Africa excludes Liberia, which was founded by freed American slaves in 1847 and still looks to the United States as the key foreign power. At the height of fighting in Monrovia in April and May, Washington confined intervention to sending troops to evacuate foreigners and protect its embassy.
After Mali Christopher goes to Ethiopia, the third-largest African recipient of U.S. aid and a bulwark against Sudan.
In Addis Ababa he will discuss how Washington can back -- financially, and not with troops -- the Organisation of African Unity's drive to end African conflicts, officials said.

U.S. diplomats in East Africa said on Thursday a planned two days in Arusha, Tanzania, meeting regional leaders had been cut to one day. They were unable to confirm Christopher would go on to Angola as planned.
In Arusha, he will discuss Burundi's crisis, refugees, other problems and cooperation with the presidents of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda and Burundi mediator Julius Nyerere of Tanzania.
Christopher had then planned to meet Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos and UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi in Launda.

But Savimbi, a former U.S. ally, refused to go to the government-held capital on Wednesday for a regional peace summit including South Africa's President Nelson Mandela, who is the photo-op highlight of Christopher's visit to Cape Town.
